name: Backtracking and Search Space Pruning
intent: Solve constraint and combination problems by building a solution one choice at a time and abandoning a branch the moment it cannot work, understand how much pruning and ordering save, and keep in mind that backtracking is still exponential in the worst case.
scenario: A solver places 8 queens on a chessboard so none attack each other. Trying every board visits 19,173,961 nodes; refusing to reuse a column visits 109,601; pruning the moment a queen is attacked visits 2,057, for the same 92 solutions. A subset-sum counter over 20 numbers drops from 2,097,151 nodes to 726,739 with pruning and 109,147 with the largest numbers tried first. Then an input arrives that pruning barely helps, and the search is exponential again.
problem: Many problems have no formula: schedules, puzzles, configurations, assignments, parsing with alternatives. They can be solved by trying choices, but the number of combinations explodes: 8 to the power 8 boards for 8 queens, 2 to the power n subsets for n items. A search that only inspects complete candidates is hopeless beyond tiny sizes. The useful insight is that a partial candidate often already violates a rule, so everything below it can be skipped, and the order in which you try choices decides how soon you find an answer.

howItWorks.title: Build the answer one choice at a time, then undo
howItWorks.text: Backtracking is a depth-first search over partial solutions. Make a choice (put a queen in this row at this column, include or skip this item), recurse to make the next one, and when that branch is exhausted undo the choice and try the next option. The recursion stack is the current partial solution. The cost to track is the number of nodes visited, one per call. With no checks until the end, 8 queens means every one of the 8 to the power 8 boards: 19,173,961 nodes in the whole tree, nearly all of them pointless.

howItWorks.title: Prune: reject a partial solution as soon as it is doomed
howItWorks.text: If two queens already attack each other, no way of placing the remaining queens repairs that, so the whole subtree under it is skipped. Testing each placement as it is made takes 8 queens from 19,173,961 nodes to 2,057, finding the same 92 solutions. Where you check matters: only forbidding reused columns (but looking at diagonals at the end) still visits 109,601 nodes, because most of the work is below placements that were already wrong. The earliest check that is cheap and correct is the best check.

howItWorks.title: Prune with bounds, not just rules
howItWorks.text: For subset sum with positive numbers, stop when the running total passes the target (taking more can only increase it) and stop when even adding every remaining item cannot reach the target. With 20 numbers that cuts 2,097,151 nodes to 726,739. These are examples of a bound: a quick estimate that proves a branch cannot contain an answer. The tighter the bound, the earlier the cut, and a bound must never cut a branch that could still hold an answer, or the search silently misses solutions.

howItWorks.title: Order the choices: fail early, succeed early
howItWorks.text: Trying the largest numbers first makes the total overshoot sooner, so the same pruning rules cut much higher in the tree: 109,147 nodes instead of 726,739 for the same 6,722 matching subsets. Order matters in another way when you only need one answer: for 24 queens, trying columns left to right reaches a first solution after 411,609 nodes, while trying the middle columns first takes 65. When you need every solution, order only moves where they are found, and the node count is unchanged: 2,057 for 8 queens either way.

howItWorks.title: It is still exponential in the worst case
howItWorks.text: Pruning changes the constant, not the shape. Pruned 8-, 9-, 10- and 11-queens cost 2,057, 8,394, 35,539 and 166,926 nodes: about four to five times more for every extra queen. For 20 items that are all equal to 2 with an unreachable odd target, the bounds almost never fire and pruning still visits 705,431 nodes against 2,097,151 without it, roughly doubling with every extra item. Treat a backtracking solver as 'fast on structured inputs, unpredictable on adversarial ones' and put a limit on its work (a node budget or a time limit) wherever the input is not under your control.

pros: General: it solves problems for which there is no formula, from puzzles to configuration and scheduling
Memory use is small: only the current partial solution is kept, proportional to the depth
Early checks can cut the work by factors of thousands, with the answers unchanged
Easy to extend with problem-specific bounds and ordering rules
cons: Exponential in the worst case: pruning rescues typical inputs, not all inputs
Performance is hard to predict from the problem size alone, because it depends on the data and on the order of choices
A wrong bound or check silently drops valid answers, and nothing reports the loss
Recursion depth can be a problem for deep searches, so deep problems may need an explicit stack
whenToUse: Constraint satisfaction with small to moderate size: puzzles, timetabling, configuration, assignment
Enumerating or counting all solutions that satisfy rules, such as permutations or subsets with a property
Problems where partial candidates can be checked cheaply and often fail early
Exact answers are needed and the instance is small enough, or well structured enough, for the search to finish
whenNotToUse: There is a polynomial algorithm or a recurrence with overlapping sub-problems: subset sum with a small target is solved by dynamic programming in time proportional to items times target
The input is untrusted and a pathological case could hang the service: use a budget, or a different method
An approximate answer from a greedy rule or a local search is acceptable and much cheaper
The search space has no early failures, so there is nothing to prune: you are paying for recursion and getting enumeration
pitfalls: Checking constraints only when a candidate is complete: 19,173,961 nodes for 8 queens against 2,057 with a check at each placement. Move the check as early as it can be done correctly
Pruning with an invalid bound, such as assuming numbers are positive when they may be negative: the search is faster and wrong, and no test fails unless it contains the missed case
Forgetting to undo a choice when backtracking: the state leaks into sibling branches and the search finds wrong or missing answers. Pair every make with an unmake in the same function
Believing a good ordering helps every goal: it moved 24 queens to its first solution in 65 nodes instead of 411,609, and changed nothing about the 2,057 nodes needed to find all 8-queens solutions
Reporting a benchmark on friendly random data: the same pruned solver visits about a third of the tree on items that defeat the bounds. Measure on the worst inputs you may actually receive
Running an unbounded search on user input: an adversarial case can make it run for hours. Add a node or time limit and decide what to return when it trips

Using backtracking where dynamic programming applies: if the same sub-problem is reached by many paths (the same remaining items and the same remaining sum), remembering it removes the repetition that pruning cannot

roles.label: Recursive search
roles.description: Makes a choice, recurses, then undoes it and tries the next option.

roles.label: Partial solution
roles.description: The choices made so far: queens placed, items included.

roles.label: Pruning check
roles.description: Rejects a partial solution as soon as no completion can work.

roles.label: Ordering heuristic
roles.description: Decides which choice to try first.

quiz.question: 8 queens need 19,173,961 nodes when every board is tried and 2,057 when each placement is checked as it is made. What explains the gap?
options: The checked version finds fewer solutions, so it has less to do.
The checked version uses a faster computer instruction for each node.
The checked version memoizes boards it has already seen.
A conflict found early removes the whole subtree beneath it from the search.
quiz.explanation: Both find the same 92 solutions. Once two queens attack each other, every way of filling the remaining rows is doomed, so none of them is visited. Checking only at the end pays for all of those nodes.

quiz.question: Columns tried from the middle outward find a first 24-queens solution in 65 nodes instead of 411,609. Will the same order speed up counting all solutions for 8 queens?
options: Yes, by about the same factor, because the order is better.
No: counting every solution visits the same 2,057 nodes in any order, since all branches must be explored.
Yes, but only when the search is also memoized.
No, because the middle-first order skips some of the solutions.
quiz.explanation: Order decides which branch holds the first answer. Counting all answers explores every branch that survives pruning, whatever the order, so the node count is unchanged. Neither order loses a solution.

quiz.question: Pruning cuts subset sum for 20 items from 2,097,151 nodes to 109,147 on random numbers, but only to 705,431 for 20 equal items with an unreachable target. What does this show?
options: The pruning code has a bug that appears only for equal items.
Equal items make the problem polynomial, so pruning is unnecessary.
How much pruning saves depends on the data, and the worst case is still exponential.
Pruning should only be used on sorted input.
quiz.explanation: The bounds cut a branch only when the total overshoots or cannot reach the target. With equal items and a target that is just out of reach, that happens late, so most of the tree survives. Guard solvers with a budget when inputs are not under your control.
